What Is a Balance Sheet? Format, Example and How to Read It

A balance sheet shows what a company owns, what it owes and what belongs to its shareholders on one specific date. This guide covers the equation behind it, its format under Indian law, and how to read it.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

The accounting equation

Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' equity. Every transaction keeps this in balance. If a company borrows ₹10 lakh, cash (an asset) rises by ₹10 lakh and borrowings (a liability) rise by the same amount.

A balance sheet is a snapshot at one date, such as 31 March. A profit and loss statement, by contrast, covers a whole period.

Format of a balance sheet in India

Indian companies follow Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, which presents equity and liabilities first, and then assets. Here is an example for Sunrise Traders Ltd (₹ lakh).

Particulars₹ lakh
Share capital100
Reserves and surplus300
Shareholders' funds400
Long-term borrowings300
Short-term borrowings50
Trade payables100
Other current liabilities50
Total equity and liabilities900
Property, plant and equipment500
Long-term investments100
Inventories120
Trade receivables100
Cash and bank80
Total assets900

Assets explained

  • Non-current assets: held for more than a year, including fixed assets, intangible assets such as goodwill, and long-term investments.
  • Current assets: expected to turn into cash within a year, including inventory, receivables, and cash.
  • Fixed assets are shown net of accumulated depreciation.

Liabilities and equity explained

  • Equity: share capital plus reserves. It is the shareholders' claim on the business and is also called net worth.
  • Non-current liabilities: due after a year, such as long-term loans and debentures.
  • Current liabilities: due within a year, such as payables and short-term borrowings.
  • Contingent liabilities: possible future obligations such as a court case, disclosed in the notes rather than on the face of the balance sheet.

What to look for

A few quick calculations from the example tell you a lot.

CheckCalculationResult
Working capital300 − 200₹100 lakh
Current ratio300 ÷ 2001.5 times
Debt-to-equity(300 + 50) ÷ 4000.875 times
Book value per share (10 lakh shares)400 ÷ 10₹40

See our guide on ratio analysis for the rest. Over several years, watch for debt growing faster than profits, receivables growing faster than sales, and large related-party balances.

Exam and interview questions

Why must a balance sheet always balance?

Because every rupee of assets has been funded by someone: either lenders (liabilities) or owners (equity). Double-entry bookkeeping records both sides of each transaction.

What is the difference between a balance sheet and a trial balance?

A trial balance lists ledger balances to check that debits equal credits. A balance sheet is a formal financial statement in a prescribed format.

Is goodwill always shown on the balance sheet?

Only goodwill arising from buying a business is recorded. Internally generated goodwill, such as a company's own reputation, is not.

Is the balance sheet a statement of market value?

No. Most assets are recorded at historical cost less depreciation, so book value can differ greatly from market value.
